transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. 

I came in because... well, I just can't stop thinking about how the left side of my face looks. It just looks completely off to me. Like my nose and my jaw are really crooked. I see it constantly—every time I look at an ID photo, or whenever I have to turn my camera on for my online college classes, it's just glaring right at me. 

It's getting really hard to deal with. Even when people tell me they don't see what I'm talking about, I just... I feel like everyone at work in the CNC lab is staring at it. I honestly feel like they're noticing how messed up my face is before they even notice the programming or the work I'm doing. I just can't stop focusing on it.
When people tell you they don't see what you're talking about, do you ever consider the possibility that your face might actually be normal and that your brain is playing a trick on you?

Honestly... no, not really. I mean, I hear them when they say it, but I just don't believe them. When I look in the mirror or at a photo, it's just so obvious to me. It's right there. 

So I don't really think my brain is playing a trick on me. I usually just assume they're trying to be nice, or... or maybe they just aren't looking at me that closely. But I know what I see.

If I were to show you a high-resolution 3D scan of your face that proved your features were perfectly symmetrical, would you be able to accept that as evidence that your perception might be inaccurate?

I don't know. I mean... with my job, I work with precise measurements and 3D models all the time, so I know how accurate that technology is supposed to be. But honestly? 

If you showed me a scan that said my face was perfectly symmetrical... I think I'd probably just assume the scanner was calibrated wrong, or that it somehow missed the specific angle where it's the most obvious. I know that probably sounds stubborn, but... I just look in the mirror and I see how crooked it is. It's so real to me. I don't think a computer image would just make me stop seeing it.

Do you find yourself doing anything specific to try to hide or fix this asymmetry, such as constantly checking mirrors, avoiding certain angles, or using your hair or clothing to cover that side of your face?

Yeah, I do a lot of that. Um, especially before I leave for school. I usually get stuck in the bathroom just... checking my face in the mirror over and over. And then I'll use my phone camera to see how it looks from different angles. 

I try to fix my hair to cover it up, or I'll keep changing my shirt to see if a different collar makes my jaw look less crooked. I also end up asking my mom if it looks weird, just... hoping she'll tell me something that makes me feel better, even though I know I won't really believe her. 

Sometimes I get so caught up doing all of this that I actually miss my lab entirely. Or if I do make it, I'm just so drained from the whole morning that I can't even focus on my programming work.
